body:
**Technical analysis more broadly**
- Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron (1992): simple moving-average and trading-range-breakout rules on the DJIA (1897-1986) had predictive power; later work (Sullivan, Timmermann & White 1999) shows much of this weakens after correcting for data snooping and in later samples. — [JF, DOI 10.1111/j.1540-6261.1992.tb04681.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1992.tb04681.x) [K]
- Lo, Mamaysky & Wang (2000): automated pattern recognition finds several technical patterns (e.g., head-and-shoulders) provide incremental information on Nasdaq stocks, though not necessarily exploitable profits. — [JF, DOI 10.1111/0022-1082.00265](https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00265) [K]
- Park & Irwin (2007) survey: of 95 "modern" studies, 56 found positive TA profits, 20 negative, 19 mixed — but many suffer data snooping, ex-post rule selection and cost-estimation problems; evidence is stronger in older samples and futures/FX than recent equities. — [Journal of Economic Surveys, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-6419.2007.00519.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-6419.2007.00519.x) [K]

body:
**Leverage and structural edge: "Buffett's Alpha" (Frazzini, Kabiller, Pedersen; FAJ 2018, vol. 74 no. 4)** [VERIFIED-PRIMARY, read from the published PDF]
- From October 1976 to March 2017, $1 in Berkshire grew to more than **$3,685**. The average excess return over T-bills was **18.6%** vs. the market's 7.5%, at **23.5% volatility** (market 15.3%). The **Sharpe ratio was 0.79** vs. the market's 0.49, beta 0.69, and information ratio 0.64. Berkshire had the highest Sharpe ratio of any US stock or mutual fund with a 40-plus-year history — [Buffett's Alpha PDF](https://gwern.net/doc/economics/2018-frazzini.pdf); [CFA Institute listing](https://rpc.cfainstitute.org/research/financial-analysts-journal/2018/ip-v3-n1-13-demystifying-buffetts-investment-success)
- **Leverage was about 1.7-to-1** (total assets to equity). Counting only equity, debt and float, it was about 1.4-to-1. The 2012 working-paper draft said about 1.6 — [PDF](https://gwern.net/doc/economics/2018-frazzini.pdf); [GuruFocus on the 2012 draft](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/614298/is-the-secret-to-buffetts-returns-leverage-)
- The average cost of insurance float was **1.72%/yr, about 3 percentage points below the T-bill rate**. Float was **about 35% of liabilities**. Debt was rated AAA from 1989 to 2009, and in 2002 Berkshire issued the first-ever negative-coupon security. Berkshire also financed capital spending with deferred taxes from accelerated depreciation ($28B in 2011) — [PDF](https://gwern.net/doc/economics/2018-frazzini.pdf)
- Leverage alone does not explain the record. 1.7x leverage on the market gives about a 12.7% excess return, well short of 18.6% — [PDF](https://gwern.net/doc/economics/2018-frazzini.pdf)
- Alpha became **statistically insignificant once betting-against-beta (BAB) and quality-minus-junk (QMJ) were controlled for**. For example, the public-stock portfolio's alpha fell to an insignificant 0.3%. A systematic "Buffett-style" portfolio of cheap, safe, quality stocks with matched leverage performed comparably — [PDF](https://gwern.net/doc/economics/2018-frazzini.pdf)
- **Public stocks did better than the wholly-owned private businesses**, which suggests his returns come more from stock selection than from his effect on management — [PDF](https://gwern.net/doc/economics/2018-frazzini.pdf)
- The authors' conclusion: "he stuck to a good strategy… for a long time period, surviving rough periods where others might have been forced into a fire sale or a career shift, and he boosted his returns by using leverage." His genius lay in "recognizing early on that these investment themes work, applying leverage without ever having a fire sale, and sticking to his principles" — [PDF](https://gwern.net/doc/economics/2018-frazzini.pdf)
- A caveat from commentary: cost-free float is not typical for the P&C industry, where premiums often fall short of claims and expenses. Berkshire's underwriting discipline made the float cheap — [GuruFocus on float](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/981189/Some-Insight-Into-How-Buffett-Has-Used-Float-to-Leverage-His-Returns-)

`case_study:polycab-2019-2026` · tickers: POLYCAB · confidence: single-source

IPO Apr 2019 at ₹538; first weekly close ₹644 → ATH ₹10,083 (Jun 2026) ≈15.7x (≈19x from the issue price). P/E 26.9 → 58.9 (2.2x) × implied EPS ~7.2x, about 28% rerating. ₹7,550 on 19 Nov 2026 (−25%), P/E ~36. Drawdowns: −45% (COVID 2020), −37% (Dec 2024–Feb 2025). Revenue FY19 ₹7,986 cr → FY26 ₹28,884 cr; OPM 12% → 14%; ROCE 22% → 33%; PAT ₹500 cr → ₹2,708 cr. Early signal (general knowledge, unverified narrative): it listed at a fair ~20–27x as the organised market leader in wires and cables while demand from real-estate, infrastructure, data centres, power transmission and exports accelerated; the FMCG-like distribution of wires and quarterly B2B/export growth were visible in investor decks. The early-2025 drop coincided with reports of a large cement group entering wires and cables, and a Dec 2023 income-tax search hit the stock briefly (both unverified). Lesson: buying a category leader at a reasonable IPO P/E lets EPS do the work. New-entrant headlines cause sharp but survivable drawdowns when ROCE keeps rising.

Key data: **start_year**: 2019; **end_year**: 2026; **start_price**: 644; **end_price**: 10083; **price_nov2026**: 7550; **multiple**: ~15.7x (~19x vs issue ₹538); **pe_start**: 26.9; **pe_end**: 58.9; **eps_multiple_implied**: ~7.2x; **max_drawdown**: -45% (2020); **early_signals**: leader listed at fair P/E; capex-cycle demand; **ended**: not ended; -25% from ATH; **lesson**: fair-priced IPO of leader; EPS-led

`insight:clean-cash-cow-funds-sick-sibling` · confidence: verified

A recurring Indian pattern: a high-quality, cash-generative listed company sits in the same group as a loss-making, capital-hungry sibling, and value moves from the first to the second through ICDs, guarantees, letters of comfort, collateral or forced promoter selling. Cases: United Spirits -> Kingfisher (SEBI 2017: ~Rs 1,880 cr diverted to UB-group entities); Zee -> Essel infra (SEBI 2023: letter-of-comfort FD adjustments; SEBI 31-Jul-2026: ZEEL's Hyderabad land mortgaged for four Essel entities' loans without authority); Jaypee Infratech -> Jaiprakash Associates (SC 2020: ~858 acres mortgaged for the parent's debt held to be preferential transactions); MIAL -> GVK group (CBI FIR 2020 alleges ~Rs 705 cr); Bajaj Consumer -> Bajaj Hindusthan/Lalitpur Power (2018-19 pledges, stake sales to fund the power business); Emami -> cement/power (2019 stake sale to repay group debt). Things to check every year: (1) RPT notes listing loans, guarantees or security given to group firms; (2) 'other financial assets' and capital advances to related parties; (3) charge filings on MCA showing listed-company assets securing other entities' loans; (4) the promoter's other businesses and their debt; (5) whether a strategic partner or buyer (Diageo at USL) later finds diversions, since they often do. Rule: the safety of a great franchise is capped by the weakest balance sheet the promoter controls.

Sources: <https://www.business-standard.com/article/pti-stories/sebi-bans-mallya-6-others-in-usl-fund-diversion-case-117012501425_1.html> · <https://www.moneylife.in/article/sebi-bars-former-zee-executives-subhash-chandra-punit-goenka-from-securities-market-for-1-year/81233.html> · <https://theprint.in/india/cbi-books-gvk-group-chairman-gvk-reddy-son-over-alleged-rs-705-crore-mumbai-airport-scam/452805> · <https://www.business-standard.com/amp/article/companies/promoters-sell-22-stake-in-bajaj-consumer-care-for-rs-700-crore-119101501423_1.html>

`insight:marks-sea-change-2022` | confidence: verified | date: 2022-12-13

Memo of 13 Dec 2022. Marks counts only three sea changes in 53 years: (1) the 1970s shift to risk/return thinking (birth of high yield, distressed debt), (2) Volcker's 1980 hike to a 20% fed funds rate that ushered in 'a declining-interest-rate environment that prevailed for four decades', and (3) the end of ultra-low rates in 2022. On 1980-2021 returns: 'I'd be surprised if 40 years of declining interest rates didn't play the greatest role of all.' 2009-21 was 'an asset owner's market and a borrower's market ... a frustrating period for lenders and bargain hunters.' Now: 'We've gone from the low-return world of 2009-21 to a full-return world'; credit can deliver 'equity-like returns, sourced from contractual cash flows', so investors 'no longer have to rely as heavily on riskier investments.' 'highly stimulative rates are likely not in the cards for the next several years, barring a serious recession.' Motto restated: 'we never know where we're going, but we ought to know where we are.' Actionable for India: valuation multiples expanded with falling global rates; in a higher-for-longer world, compare equity earnings yields with Indian G-sec/AAA yields (~6.5-7.5%) and don't assume multiple expansion in return models.

Sources:
- https://www.oaktreecapital.com/insights/memo/sea-change
